Beyond this, most of the novel is about the violence and the ability to fall for a con in so-called American civilization. Mark Twain also critiques church people who will give for distant missions but not take care of their local poor. Huck finally rejects "civilization" and heads west. I love Huck Finn. The novel is about racism, and also about something more: the slippery, self-serving nature of morality. (Or, as Huck puts it, “what's the use you learning to do right when it's troublesome to do right and ain't no trouble to do wrong, and the wages is just the same?") It is also about the absurdities, and discontents, of civilization, seen in Huck's ineradicable unease at the prospect of being assimilated into society, and in the elusive vision of finding peace off the grid: "I was powerful glad to get away . . . , and so was Jim . . . . We said there wasn't no home like a raft, after all. Other places do seem so cramped up and smothery, but a raft don't. You feel mighty free and easy and comfortable on a raft."

For a brilliant and revelatory perspective, see Toni Morrison's essay on what she calls "this amazing troubling book." https://www.uctenglish.com/uploads/1/3/6/0/13601377/this_amazing_troubling_book.pdf

comments.name: Valued Shopper
comments.body: The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was required reading in my high school, and I digested it without too much thinking. I do not remember the plight of black people or civil rights discussed much at all in my suburban high school outside a midwestern city with a large black population. Unless these works are taught with care and precision, simply reading them and leaving students to their own interpretations isn't going to be helpful. I went on to study history in college and received my degree. It wasn't until my son came home with a tattoo that said "The Black Wall Street" that I came to be more curious. Despite my education, I truly did not know what the Black Wall Street was until I researched it on the internet. I would say that was the day I became "woke" perhaps? We should not censor Huckleberry Finn. We should teach it carefully and give students an understanding of what the book was trying to do in a terrible time in our nation's history. Then we need to come to terms with the evils of our Republic, and that our experience is  not superior from totalitarian regimes we used to be quick to criticize, but now embrace.

According to this account, Trump was warned before the attack that killing Iran’s supreme leader could produce a more hard-line regime, trigger an attempt to close the Strait of Hormuz, hammer global energy markets, and put U.S. forces and allies at risk.

And we’ve seen this movie before: “Russian collusion,” “Hunter Biden’s laptop is Russian disinformation,” “Biden is sharp as a tack,” and countless other media narratives presented with absolute certainty—until inconvenient facts got in the way.

Journalists get things wrong. That’s inevitable. What’s harder to excuse is the certainty with which these narratives are presented, the repetition that turns speculation into “fact,” and the conspicuous lack of urgency when the story eventually falls apart.

The lesson? Be skeptical when digesting today’s news. Read beyond the headline, question the narrative, and remember that yesterday’s “settled fact” can become tomorrow’s correction.

When law enforcement agencies normally raid drug suppliers, interdict ground transportation of drugs, or stop seagoing vessels carrying drugs, the people are arrested, and the drugs confiscated. Why? Because the people - low level criminals - can be persuaded to give up information about higher levels of the organization, which can lead to actually shutting down - even if only temporarily - their criminal enterprise. 
And the drugs themselves can be used as evidence against those people at the higher levels. More immediately, the drugs and their containers or packaging may furnish clues about their origin and routes.
So, why this expenditure of expensive weapons to blow to smithereens small boats and people who are unlikely to be the ringleaders in the drug trade? 
If a domestic drug enforcement agency such as the DEA were to conduct raids this way, using large amounts of lethal and destructive weaponry that resulted in the complete loss of all evidence and death of every suspect, one would be well justified in wondering what they were trying to hide. If your local police force raided a drug house and incinerated all of the drugs and paraphernalia without using it as evidence against the criminals, you might well speculate that something fishy was going on.

I study head-impact biomechanics--i.e., the features of an impact that could explain injury, the mechanical response of the brain to that impact, and the microstructural changes that follow TBI and repetitive head impacts.

Football is a tail-risk problem with potentially catastrophic consequences.

I.e., there is a very good chance that a child who plays football, even if he reaches the professional level, will go on to live a healthy and productive life, never develop symptomatic CTE, and die of old age.

But there is also a non-negligible but smaller chance where one head-impact event, or the cumulative effects of repeated impacts, lead to profound life-altering consequences like post-concussive syndrome and neurodegenerative disease, i.e, cte, als, parkinsons, dementia etc.

And we still cannot identify, ahead of time, who is in which risk category.

So how should a parent weigh a low-probability but potentially devastating outcome? I dont know -

Opium dens, where it was smoked, were brought by Chinese immigants. This all created a smoldering addiction problem. The invention of injectable morphine in the civil war was the spark that turned this into a raging inferno. Everyone was stoned. The Safe Food and Drug Act of 1906 came in response. A key objective of this act was to get opiates out of consumer goods. The second wave was the Vietnam war, when surving soldiers sent to Asia were exposed to readily available heroin, and came home with addiction. By the late 70s we had a war on drugs and medical schools taught the high risks of opiate addiction. Pain was not to be treated aggressively in the more enlightened  schools of the day. The third wave hit in the mid 90s when Purdue pharma managed to bamboozle a new generation of physicians at scale into thinking about pain as "the 5th vital sign" and to treat it aggressively. The rates of addiction skyrocketed. The illicit trade saw the opportunity and moved in to take advantage. After each of these waves, the problems of addiction have hit communities of poverty extremely hard, where they run like festering wounds. The only hope, in my opinion , is to prevent the 4th wave. It is quite difficult for me to believe that the 25th anniversary is almost upon us.  For me, this tragedy still feels very recent, as though I could turn around and touch it.

I was still a teenager, eagerly anticipating my future, on that bright blue morning a quarter century ago.  I woke up in my college dorm and looked out the window and thought how blue and clear the sky was.  My roommate was still asleep.  And then, the news on TV: the World Trade Center towers billowing smoke and fire.  I was terrified that it was the end of the world.  Perhaps I can be forgiven for that, because I was only 19 and no one expects to see mass murder on live television, or anywhere.  A few days later I woke up in the middle of the night, terrified, but unable to name the terror: was just there.

I'm 44 now.  I sometimes think that all the people whose lives were snuffed out 25 years ago next month were meant to interact with us all somehow, that there were people we were all supposed to meet, even briefly, befriend, love, etc., and now we never will. Those terrorists permanently altered the psychic ecosystem of the entire planet, because one person's life touches the next, and the ripples reverberate into eternity.  So much was lost. And the potential for our country was lost, too.  We'll never know whom we could have been, and that is the ultimate tragedy.

As we approach this 25th anniversary, I wish us solace. The dead have already achieved that peace which passeth all understanding.

Suddenly we heard a deep grounding sound , we both looked at each other and my colleague asked in wonderment about the sound.  My desk was next to the window, I got up to look, but could not see that far up to the WTC.  I remembered there was an attack a couple of years back. I yelled to no one in particular it was a bomb. We took matters into our own hand and walked down swiftly forty two flights down to the street. Where I live, a 11,000 Volt cable was buried inches below the road (it's supposed to be at least 3' below the ground, but hey, no one was looking when they installed the cable). The electric company claimed that they could not bury the cable deeper due to a massive granite formation. 

Rolling vehicular traffic would squeeze the shallow cable and cause breakages. Frequently. Leading to neighborhood power cuts and excavations to re-join the broken cable. These excavations, on a narrow, busy street, would hold up traffic. Major inconvenience. Street scuffles, chaos, madness.

A group of us took it up on ourselves to figure out just where the granite rock began. We dug below the cable, and, lo and behold, inches below the cable, we found a ductile iron water pipe. There was no massive granite formation that made it impossible to dig further; the cable broke because it was getting pinched between the pipe below and vehicular tires above.  

The water and electricity departments argued over who should pay for reburying the pipe and cable deeper. A massive excavation and re-work eventually took place. Both cable and pipe are now at safe depths. Excavations are rarer, traffic has calmed down a notch.

This happened in Bangalore, India, where chaos is normal and government service is expected to be sclerotic. I am both surprised and heartened to know that as modern and developed a city as NYC has the same issue of official ignorance of underground works.

The US already imports magnesium from Canada.  This is for two reasons:

1) Permitting Speed: Establishing new mining or refining operations in the U.S. is notoriously slow, taking an average of 7 to 10 years to secure permits. By comparison, Canada’s streamlined regulatory system averages just 2 years.

2) Cheaper Energy Supply: Refining magnesium is an incredibly energy-intensive process. Canada has readily available and affordable hydroelectric power infrastructure, making metal smelting significantly cheaper than in most parts of the U.S.

It makes more sense for the US to import from an ally than from China, and a lot more sense to work with Canada than to fight with them.

Canada accounts for roughly 24% of U.S. magnesium scrap imports, whereas China supplies approximately 20% of U.S. magnesium scrap imports. However, for primary pure magnesium metal, the U.S. imports 0% from China due to anti-dumping tariffs, relying instead on countries like Israel.

comments.body: In the summer of 1824, the Marquis de Lafayette returned to America after an absence of 40 years. The aging hero's reappearance inspired one of the grandest and most colorful celebrations in the nation's history. The pageantry, the pomp, the Lafayette merchandise, are all fun and fascinating. But the event had a deeper significance: During his 13-month tour, the Nation's Guest stirred up unifying nostalgia for the past, affirmed the young republic's many successes, but also encouraged its citizens to better live up to their founding ideals. Two centuries on, the story of Lafayette's last visit reminds us still what citizenship in a self-governing state requires and how we can both commemorate and be clear-eyed about American history.

They lost 1/3 of the Abrams that we gave them in a single day, attempting a daylight drive literally up the middle of a Russian defensive line. UK advisors and US trainers (in Poland) were aghast at the loss and poor tactics. Additionally, the use of armor for artillery support is stupid - no Western tank effectively does what an artillery or mortar tube can do for a fraction of the cost.  Of course much of the battle area is thicket and swampy regions where Infantry always dominates, begging the question of why the original focus. Now it seems we've reached a strategic stalemate, and drone and trenches are the only form of warfare now used.

comments.name: Connor
comments.body:
One of the key reasons these Western tanks were so desired was the emphasis on crew survivability. The Russian T-72 series utilizes an autoloading turret that stores the ammunition inside the turret ring. Look up "Turret toss" to see what happens when that vehicle is hit by anti-tank weaponry. 

No, drones do not mean the end of the tank. Armored vehicles still have a role in the modern battlefield. They were used in the Kursk salient in 2024. Russia continues to use (and lose) theirs. At the very least, a tank is mobile fire support, somewhere between the "grenade launcher" and "artillery" range. The Challenger 2 was used in such a role. 

It could be argued that a better platform is the infantry fighting vehicle or armored personnel carriers, like the Bradley Fighting Vehicle, which carries a 25mm autocannon, a pair of TOW anti-tank weapons, and can hold troops - and keep them alive under fire. 

Just because the current situation on the battlefield is not a good environment for Ukraine's tanks, does not mean they are not valuable.

comments.name: EEngineer & Army Aviator
comments.body:
The culprit is mechanical damage to the battery, either during manufacture or more likely during use.  If a phone or laptop has a dented or even slightly bent case, the battery may be damaged.  If it is damaged, the chances of fire during any operation, charging or discharging are higher.

Don't put your phones in your pants pocket or stuffed purse.  Don't put your laptop in an overstuffed bag.  Keep both phones and laptops in separate compartments in your travel bags and purses, preferably ones with some rigid or semi-rigid stiffeners in the sides.  In purses, the middle most compartment is generally safer.

I have no data to support the following, but my personal belief as an electrical engineer is that in flight power from your seat is safer than using a battery pack, because battery packs may use lower quality batteries.

comments.name: Mark H
comments.body: The thing about open-weight AI models is that developers and users can use one on their own machine, depending upon what their needs are. There are advantages to doing so. First is cost. There are LLM models out there that will run on a smartphone, laptop, or PC without having to purchase additional hardware and that are free to download and use. I have one installed on my PC. I do not have to have a subscription or pay for token use. Second is because I can run one on my PC, it reduces the need to having to build large data centers and infrastructure to support them.  I also run Linux, which is also open source software. Open source/open weight means that there will be more people looking at the code and finding and correcting flaws before they become a problem or cause serious damage. That can't be done with closed source/closed weight models, just look at the history of Microsoft Windows.

comments.name: Steven Sar
comments.body:
The salient facts are that Mr. Lane was Forbes' "editor in chief" and that "in 2016 Lane helped to facilitate the partnership between Forbes Media and Shook Research". Previously, "Lane and Shook developed a friendship in 2011".

Without Lane disclosing the transaction  to Forbes, "private-equity firm PPC Enterprises acquired a majority stake in Shook Research last summer.

And, also unbeknownst to Forbes, "Lane assisted in the Shook Research [majority ownership] sales effort by speaking about the relationship between that company and the magazine during the due diligence stage".

Presumably, Lane gave the prospective acquirer assurances about how solid  and continuing Shook's business relationship with Forbes were, especially with Lane as editor in chief.

And if Lane had any foreknowledge that Shook would "make a payment" to him conditioned on the PPC purchase closing, he could be described as an agent with two masters, Forbes and PPC.

Conspicuously absent from the article is any statement by PPC about whether they knew Lane would be paid if the deal with Shook was completed or about what if anything Lane said during PPC's "due diligence" inquiries about the future durability of the Shook-Forbes "partnership".

Lane describes his actions and omissions an "error in judgment". But depending on the results of a fuller investigation, that could be a monumental understatement.

This article fails to take into account the fact that corporations see cybersecurity as a cost overhead to be managed. A succession of large hacks, like the Target point-of-sale a decade ago, show almost criminal neglect and fatal overconfidence. Outdated software, uninstalled patches, outdated hardware. These new A.I. models will find the weak corporate links and there will be an explosion of successful hacks from criminal gangs at home and abroad. 

This is the same nativity we see when Flock executives tell us their cameras are fine as long as the police don’t abuse them. We know what the reality is. Silicon Valley doesn’t care that their products are weaponized to do harm. They only care about revenue and profit.

"Businesses and individuals, these experts say, can use the same A.I. technologies to defend themselves against cyberattacks."

"Open weight systems like GLM 5.3 will allow everyone to defend themselves — not just a chosen few."

With little exception, individuals do not have the time or capacity to "use A.I. ... to defend themselves".  At best, individuals with available $$ can gamble on buying a hopefully strong defensive capability from a corporation.  One that they won't be able to understand, evaluate, control, or configure.

Suppose an attacker decides to raid bank accounts at a financial institution. The account holders need to trust that protection software chosen and deployed by that institution is powerful and most probably in place after a testing period. Who do you think can move quicker? Plus, at the breath-taking speed with which these hacking reports are being issued how can the public have confidence in any alleged remedy?

Ms Friedman is a great example of how we should treat growing older. Keep doing something you love. 
My mother’s first love is music. As a young girl sent off to boarding school, she found solace in music and as an adult, taught music all her life. 
That passion kept her going till the age of 88, when failing health and hearing loss forced her to retire. She’s 92 now and bedridden, but she had created enduring memories and inculcated in me, a lifelong love for music. 
I hope Ms Friedman continues to do what she loves. More power to her.

comments.name: Retired in CT
comments.body: Lily was my piano teacher when I was a teenager and she established such a helpful foundation for my playing that, throughout my business career and now in retirement, playing piano and organ is still my greatest joy.  I was delighted to see this article about her this morning and also not surprised to learn she was still actively playing.  She shared with me the same drive that has kept her at the piano all these years; it is difficult to put into words, but I can say it's as though the idea music should be a part of your every day life goes without saying.  With the skills I learned from Lily 50+ years ago, I have a thoroughly engaging avocation in retirement that is self-nourishing.  The largest room in our home is the music room, and I enjoy having musicians of all stripes play for us and our friends.  Just last week we had nearly 100 people here for a performance.  And it all started with Lilly.  When you count up all of her students and audience members over nearly a century, think of how many people the devotion to her craft has reached and how many lives have been improved over that time, even if just a little.  We need many more people in this world like her.

This is a very touching and meaningful story. I am inspired by Ms. Friedman. I believe that while the body ages, the spirit literally does not. Being, consciousness, awareness, spirit, soul, etc., is in the same pristine shape at age 95 that it was at age 9. Ms. Friedman appears to feel this way. 

The literature is very demanding. Beethoven’s Opus 111 is a very challenging work at any age, and not just the extended trills to conclude the second movement. 
I am 65, and I have no plans to retire from my position as Director of Sacred Music at a church.  Afterall, Charles Widor served as organist at Saint-Sulpice in Paris for 63 years. But I know, and I have always known, that the demands of my job as organist, pianist, and conductor, are slight compared to the demands of performing the pianist’s repertoire. Having performed major works of Beethoven, Schumann, Scriabin, etc., I know what is required. And that is why I am in such awe of Ms. Friedman. I cannot imagine doing it in my 90’s, but her story encourages me to persevere. 

Ms. Friedman: Here’s to many more years of an astonishing career. Your story inspires people, like myself, who have not personally met you.
